unit.title: Business Models & Growth
unit.summary: How products make money and grow: business models and pricing, unit economics, growth loops, go-to-market and product-market fit.

lessons.title: Business models and monetisation
objectives: Describe common business models: subscription, transaction, marketplace, freemium and ads
Match a monetisation model to user behaviour and value

explanation.en: A business model describes how a product creates, delivers and captures value. Common models: subscriptions (recurring fee), transactions (a fee per use), marketplaces (a commission on trades between buyers and sellers), freemium (free core with paid upgrades) and advertising (users pay with attention). Good monetisation charges in a way that aligns with the value users get.
explanation.ta: Business model-na: oru product eppadi value-a create panni, deliver panni, capture pannudhu-nu describe pannum. Common models: subscription (adikkadi kattura fee), transaction (ovvoru use-kkum fee), marketplace (vaangubavar–virpavar trade-la commission), freemium (core free, upgrades-ku kaasu), advertising (users attention-aala kaasu kattuvaanga). Nalla monetisation, users-ku kidaikkura value-oda align aagura vazhila charge pannum.

analogy.en: A gym can charge monthly (subscription), per visit (transaction), take a cut from personal trainers (marketplace), or offer free outdoor sessions and paid classes (freemium).
analogy.ta: Gym maasa fee vaangalaam (subscription), ovvoru visit-kkum (transaction), personal trainers-kitta cut edukkalaam (marketplace), illa free outdoor sessions-um paid classes-um (freemium).

takeaway.en: Charge for the value metric customers care about, in a way that grows as they get more value.
takeaway.ta: Customers mukkiyamaa ninaikkura value metric-ku charge pannunga — avangalukku value adhigamaaga, kattanam-um adhigamaagura maadhiri.

deep.title: Why it matters for PMs
deep.body: Product decisions shape revenue: what's free versus paid, when the paywall appears, what's included in each plan. A brilliant product with the wrong monetisation can fail, and aggressive monetisation can destroy trust and retention.

deep.title: Models and their trade-offs
deep.body: Subscription: predictable revenue; must deliver ongoing value or churn rises. Transaction fees: scale with usage; sensitive to competition. Marketplace commission (‘take rate’): must create value for both sides; disintermediation risk (users take deals offline). Freemium: wide adoption; typically only a small share converts, so the free tier must create upgrade demand without being useless. Advertising: free for users; needs huge scale and risks a worse experience and privacy concerns.

deep.title: Pricing approaches
deep.body: Cost-plus (cost + margin) ignores value. Competitor-based follows the market. Value-based prices according to the value delivered to customers, ideally tied to a ‘value metric’ — per seat, per transaction, per GB — that grows with customer success. Test willingness to pay through research methods such as Van Westendorp surveys, pricing-page experiments or sales conversations.

deep.title: Context: Indian markets
deep.body: Price sensitivity, UPI-driven small payments, sachet pricing (small, frequent purchases), and strong free alternatives shape monetisation. Many products in India succeed with low-priced plans, pay-per-use options and annual plans timed to salary or festival cycles.

lessons.example: Illustrative example: a photo-editing app offers basic editing free, with premium filters and high-resolution export in a paid plan. Its value metric is exports: casual users stay free, while creators who export often see clear value in paying.
lessons.counterexample: A note-taking app that puts a paywall on the second note — users never experience enough value to want to pay.
mistakes: Pricing by cost instead of value
A free tier so generous nobody upgrades, or so limited nobody stays
Ignoring how monetisation affects retention and trust

keyTerms.meaning: A free core product with paid premium features.
The percentage a marketplace keeps from each transaction.
The unit of value customers pay for, which grows with their success.

questions.prompt: Which model makes money from commissions on trades between buyers and sellers?

options.text: Pricing according to the value customers receive

questions.prompt: A freemium app converts 0.3% of users to paid; most say the free version does everything they need. What's the best lever?

options.text: Rethink the free/paid boundary so premium features target the needs of the most engaged users
options.why: Right — the paywall boundary determines upgrade demand.
May hurt the experience without fixing conversion.

questions.explanation: Design the free tier to create upgrade moments.

questions.prompt: In a home-services marketplace, many customers book a plumber once and then contact them directly. What's this risk, and a response?

options.text: Disintermediation — add ongoing value through the platform: guarantees, easy payments, rebooking, insurance
options.why: Yes — make staying on the platform worth it for both sides.

questions.explanation: Marketplaces must keep creating value for both sides.

exercise.scenario: You're designing monetisation for a PM-learning app like this one.
exercise.prompt: Propose a model, define the free and paid tiers, choose a value metric and name one risk with mitigation.
exercise.modelAnswer: Model: freemium subscription. Free: the full foundations curriculum, daily lessons and spaced reviews — enough to build the habit and trust. Paid (monthly or annual, priced for Indian learners): advanced units (AI PM, strategy), unlimited interview mock sessions with detailed feedback, and portfolio case templates. Value metric: interview-preparation depth, which grows as users near job searches. Risk: users pay only around interview season and churn after. Mitigation: annual plans with a discount, and career-stage content (first 90 days as a PM) that extends value after landing a job.
checklist: Paid tier aligns with a value metric

lessons.title: Unit economics: CAC, LTV and margins
objectives: Calculate CAC, LTV and contribution margin
Interpret the LTV:CAC ratio and payback period
Use unit economics in product decisions

explanation.en: Unit economics asks whether you make or lose money on each customer or order. CAC (customer acquisition cost) is what you spend to win a customer. LTV (lifetime value) is the profit a customer brings over their lifetime — roughly margin per period × expected lifetime. If LTV is comfortably above CAC (a common rule of thumb is 3:1), growth is sustainable.
explanation.ta: Unit economics kekkuradhu: ovvoru customer illa order-la laabamaa nashtamaa? CAC (customer acquisition cost) — oru customer-a pidikka neenga selavu panradhu. LTV (lifetime value) — oru customer avanga lifetime-la kondu varra laabam — sumaar ovvoru period margin × ethirpaakkura lifetime. LTV, CAC-a vida comfortable-ah adhigam-na (common rule of thumb 3:1), growth sustainable.

analogy.en: A tea stall owner who spends ₹50 on flyers to attract a customer who buys one ₹10 tea and never returns is losing money on every customer.
analogy.ta: ₹50 flyers-ku selavu panni, ore oru ₹10 tea kudichittu thirumba varaadha customer-a pidikkura tea kadai owner, ovvoru customer-layum nashtam paarkiraar.

takeaway.en: Growth only creates value when each customer is worth more than they cost to acquire and serve.
takeaway.ta: Ovvoru customer-um avangala pidikka, serve panna aagura selavai vida adhiga mathippu kondadhaa irundhaa dhaan growth value create pannum.

deep.title: Key formulas
deep.body: CAC = total acquisition spend ÷ new customers acquired in the period. Contribution margin per order = revenue − variable costs (delivery, payment fees, discounts, support). Simple LTV = average contribution margin per month × average customer lifetime in months (lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ monthly churn rate). Payback period = CAC ÷ monthly contribution margin per customer.

deep.title: Worked example
deep.body: A subscription app spends ₹6,00,000 on marketing and gains 2,000 subscribers: CAC = ₹300. Each pays ₹199 per month with ₹40 variable cost, so contribution is ₹159 per month. Monthly churn of 10% gives an expected lifetime of about 10 months, so LTV ≈ ₹1,590. LTV:CAC ≈ 5.3:1, and payback ≈ 300 ÷ 159 ≈ 1.9 months — healthy, if the churn estimate holds.

deep.title: How product decisions move unit economics
deep.body: Retention improvements raise LTV. Better onboarding and referrals lower CAC. Operational efficiency (batching deliveries, cheaper payment methods, fewer support contacts) raises margin. Discounts lower margin and can attract low-retention users. PMs should model the economic effect of major features.

deep.title: Pitfalls
deep.body: Blended CAC hides expensive channels — calculate it per channel. LTV based on optimistic, unproven lifetimes. Ignoring the time value of money and long paybacks. And confusing revenue with contribution: high-revenue orders can still lose money.

lessons.example: Illustrative example: a quick-commerce service finds that orders below ₹200 have negative contribution after delivery cost. It introduces a small-cart fee and bundles suggestions to raise basket size, improving contribution without hurting overall order volume much.
lessons.counterexample: Celebrating growth from a ₹500 cashback campaign while each acquired user spends ₹300 in total before churning.
mistakes: Ignoring variable costs like discounts and delivery

keyTerms.meaning: Customer acquisition cost: spend to acquire one customer.
Lifetime value: total contribution a customer generates over their lifetime.
Revenue minus variable costs for an order or customer.
Time to recover CAC from a customer's contribution.

questions.prompt: ₹10 lakh marketing spend brings 5,000 new customers. What's the CAC?
With 5% monthly churn, what's the approximate average customer lifetime?
Channel A: CAC ₹150, LTV ₹600. Channel B: CAC ₹400, LTV ₹500. Where should you shift budget?

options.text: Toward A (4:1) and away from B (1.25:1), while checking A can scale
Toward B because LTV is similar

questions.prompt: A feature reduces monthly churn from 10% to 8%. What happens to LTV (all else equal)?

options.text: It rises about 25% (lifetime goes from 10 to 12.5 months)
options.why: Yes — small churn improvements have big LTV effects.

questions.explanation: Retention is a powerful LTV lever.

exercise.scenario: A meal-subscription startup charges ₹2,500 per month. Food and delivery cost ₹1,900 per month per customer. Monthly churn is 12%. CAC is ₹3,000.
exercise.prompt: Calculate contribution, lifetime, LTV, LTV:CAC and payback, assess health, and propose two product levers.
exercise.modelAnswer: Contribution = ₹2,500 − ₹1,900 = ₹600 per month. Lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ 0.12 ≈ 8.3 months. LTV ≈ ₹600 × 8.3 ≈ ₹5,000. LTV:CAC ≈ 1.7:1 — weak. Payback = ₹3,000 ÷ ₹600 = 5 months, which is a large share of the 8-month lifetime. Levers: 1) reduce churn with menu personalisation and easy pause instead of cancel (raises lifetime); 2) lower delivery cost by batching deliveries by neighbourhood and time slot (raises contribution). Also check CAC per channel and push referrals, which tend to be cheaper.
checklist: Levers target LTV, margin or CAC

lessons.title: Growth: AARRR and growth loops
objectives: Explain growth loops and why they beat linear funnels
Design a referral or content loop

explanation.en: AARRR maps the customer lifecycle: Acquisition (they find you), Activation (first value), Retention (they come back), Referral (they bring others) and Revenue (they pay). Growth loops are cycles where the output of one user's activity brings in new users — for example, shared content attracting new viewers who also create and share. Loops compound; one-off campaigns don't.
explanation.ta: AARRR customer lifecycle-a map pannum: Acquisition (ungala kandupidikkiraanga), Activation (mudhal value), Retention (thirumba varaanga), Referral (mathavangala kootittu varaanga), Revenue (kaasu kattuvaanga). Growth loops-na: oru user-oda activity-oda output pudhu users-a kondu varra cycle — udhaaranam share panna content pudhu viewers-a izhukkum, avangalum create panni share pannuvaanga. Loops compound aagum; one-time campaigns aagaadhu.

analogy.en: A campaign is like pushing a swing once; a loop is like a swing that pumps itself higher each time.
analogy.ta: Campaign oru thadavai oonjal-a thallura maadhiri; loop ovvoru thadavaiyum thaane innum uyarama poga pump panra oonjal maadhiri.

takeaway.en: Find the stage where users leak most, and look for loops where user activity naturally brings new users.
takeaway.ta: Users adhigama ozhugura stage-a kandupidinga; user activity iyalbaave pudhu users-a kondu varra loops-a thedunga.

deep.title: AARRR as a diagnostic
deep.body: Dave McClure's ‘pirate metrics’ help locate the bottleneck. Huge acquisition with poor activation means the onboarding or value promise is broken. Good activation with poor retention means the ongoing value is weak. Fix stages in order of impact; pouring users into a leaky retention stage wastes money.

deep.title: Types of growth loops
deep.body: Viral loops: users invite others because the product works better together (payments, messaging) or for rewards (referral credits). Content loops: users create content that search engines or social platforms surface to new users (reviews, Q&A). Paid loops: revenue from users funds more acquisition — works when LTV exceeds CAC. Sales loops: customers expand usage, producing case studies that win more customers.

deep.title: Designing a referral loop
deep.body: 1) A natural sharing moment (after a success, such as a completed order). 2) Clear value for both sides (a double-sided reward or inherent value of being together). 3) Low friction (one-tap share via WhatsApp). 4) Smooth onboarding for the invited person. 5) Measurement: invites sent per user, invite acceptance, activation of invited users. Viral coefficient K = invites per user × conversion; K > 1 means self-sustaining growth, which is rare.

deep.title: Growth ethics
deep.body: Avoid dark patterns: spammy contact uploads, misleading rewards, guilt-tripping notifications. They may boost short-term numbers but damage trust and retention, and they can violate privacy laws.

lessons.example: Illustrative example: a UPI payments app has a built-in viral loop — to pay a friend, the friend may need the app or a compatible UPI app; every payment exposes the brand to new users. A cashback referral adds an incentive on top of the inherent loop.
lessons.counterexample: A referral programme offering ₹200 to both sides that attracts users who cash out the bonus and never return, raising CAC without retention.
mistakes: Spending on acquisition while retention is broken
Referral rewards that attract fraud or low-intent users

keyTerms.meaning: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue — pirate metrics.
A self-reinforcing cycle where user activity produces new users.
New users each user brings in: invites per user × conversion rate.

questions.prompt: A product gets many sign-ups, but few users experience core value. Which AARRR stage is weak?
Each user sends 4 invites, and 20% convert. What's K?
A recipe app wants a content loop. Which design fits best?

options.text: Let users publish recipes and reviews that are searchable on the web, linking new visitors to the app
options.why: User content is discovered by new users who create more content.
That's paid acquisition, not a content loop.

questions.explanation: Content loops turn creation into acquisition.

questions.prompt: Retention after week 1 is 8%. Marketing wants to double the acquisition budget. What's your advice?

options.text: Fix activation and retention first; more acquisition into a leaky bucket wastes money

options.why: Users who don't stay won't refer much.

exercise.scenario: A study-group app helps college students prepare for exams together.
exercise.prompt: Identify a natural growth loop, describe its steps, list the metrics you'd track and one risk.
exercise.modelAnswer: Loop: a student creates a study group for an upcoming exam → invites classmates via WhatsApp (they need the app to join the shared notes and quizzes) → invited classmates join, study and later create groups for other subjects → those groups invite more classmates. Metrics: groups created per active user, invites per group, invite acceptance rate, activation of invited users (joined a session within 48 hours), and groups created by invited users. Risk: spammy invites annoying students — mitigate by keeping invites user-initiated and context-specific.
checklist: Loop is natural to the product's value

lessons.title: Go-to-market and product-market fit
objectives: Explain product-market fit and how to measure it
Outline a go-to-market plan: segment, positioning, channels, pricing
Recognise when to scale versus keep iterating

explanation.en: Product-market fit (PMF) means a product satisfies a strong need for a specific market so well that users keep coming back and recommend it. Signals: retention curves that flatten, organic word of mouth and the ‘very disappointed’ test (a common benchmark: 40%+ of users would be very disappointed if they could no longer use it). Go-to-market (GTM) is how you bring a product to customers: target segment, positioning, channels, pricing and launch plan.
explanation.ta: Product-market fit (PMF)-na: oru specific market-oda strong need-a product evlo nallaa satisfy pannudhu-na, users thirumba thirumba varaanga, mathavangalukku recommend pannuraanga. Signals: flat aagura retention curves, organic word of mouth, ‘very disappointed’ test (common benchmark: 40%+ users ‘idhu illaina romba disappointed aaven’-nu solluvaanga). Go-to-market (GTM) — product-a customers-kitta eppadi kondu poradhu: target segment, positioning, channels, pricing, launch plan.

analogy.en: PMF is when the restaurant has a queue outside without advertising; GTM is how you got the first people in the door.
analogy.ta: Advertisement illaama restaurant veliya queue nikkudhu-na adhu PMF; mudhal customers-a ulla kondu vandha vazhi dhaan GTM.

takeaway.en: Don't scale go-to-market spend before retention shows real fit in your target segment.
takeaway.ta: Target segment-la retention real fit-a kaattura varai GTM spend-a scale pannaadheenga.

deep.title: Measuring PMF
deep.body: No single number proves PMF. Combine: retention curves that flatten at a healthy level for your category; the Sean Ellis survey (‘How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?’ — the 40% ‘very disappointed’ benchmark is a rule of thumb); organic growth through referrals; and qualitative pull (customers asking for more, complaining when it's down). Measure within your target segment, not across all users.

deep.title: Before PMF vs after PMF
deep.body: Before: focus on learning, a narrow segment, rapid iteration, manual tactics that don't scale (personal onboarding, founder-led sales). After: focus on scaling acquisition channels, operational reliability, adjacent segments and efficiency. Scaling before PMF burns money and can bury the signal.

deep.title: GTM plan components
deep.body: 1) Target segment and ideal customer profile. 2) Positioning and messaging. 3) Pricing and packaging. 4) Channels: product-led (self-serve, viral), sales-led (B2B), partnerships, community, content, paid. 5) Launch sequencing: beta, limited release, general availability. 6) Success metrics for each stage. 7) Readiness: support, documentation, sales enablement.

deep.title: Product-led vs sales-led
deep.body: Product-led growth relies on users discovering, trying and buying the product themselves (common for low-price, simple products). Sales-led relies on sales teams (common for complex, high-price B2B). Many companies blend them: self-serve for small teams, sales for enterprises.

lessons.example: Illustrative example: a B2B invoicing tool for Indian freelancers finds strong retention among designers and developers who invoice foreign clients. It narrows GTM to that segment: positioning around ‘get paid internationally, GST-ready’, channels through freelancer communities and YouTube tutorials, and a low monthly price with a free trial.
lessons.counterexample: Spending crores on TV ads for an app whose 30-day retention is 3%.
mistakes: Measuring PMF across all users instead of the target segment
Choosing channels that don't match the product's price and complexity

keyTerms.meaning: Product-market fit: strong demand and retention in a specific market.
Go-to-market: the plan for reaching and winning customers.
Growth driven by users adopting the product themselves.
Ideal customer profile: the customer type you can best serve and win.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest evidence of PMF?

options.text: Retention curves flattening at a healthy level in the target segment, plus organic referrals

questions.explanation: Retention and organic pull signal fit.

questions.prompt: When does product-led growth typically fit best?

options.text: Simple, lower-priced products users can adopt on their own
Complex enterprise systems needing long procurement

questions.explanation: Match the channel to the product's complexity and price.

questions.prompt: Survey: 22% of all users say ‘very disappointed’, but 48% of freelance designers do. What's the implication?

options.text: You may have PMF in the freelance-designer segment; focus GTM there

questions.prompt: Your app has strong retention in Bengaluru. Leadership wants to launch in 20 cities next month. What's prudent?

options.text: Expand in stages — a few similar cities first — checking that retention and operations hold before scaling further
options.why: Validates fit in new markets while limiting risk.
Expansion is the next step after fit.

questions.explanation: Fit in one market doesn't guarantee fit in all.

exercise.scenario: You're launching an AI-powered resume-review feature in a job app for fresh graduates.
exercise.prompt: Write a mini GTM plan: segment, positioning statement, two channels, pricing approach, launch stages and success metrics per stage.
exercise.modelAnswer: Segment: final-year engineering and commerce students in tier-1 and tier-2 cities applying for first jobs. Positioning: ‘For final-year students applying for their first job, ResumeCheck gives instant, specific feedback that makes your resume recruiter-ready in 10 minutes. Unlike generic templates, it explains what to fix and why.’ Channels: college placement-cell partnerships; short Instagram and YouTube tutorials. Pricing: 2 free reviews, then a low-priced pack during placement season. Stages: beta with 3 colleges (metric: users who apply edits and rate feedback useful), limited launch in 20 colleges (week-2 return rate, paid conversion), general launch (organic referrals, interview-call self-reports).
checklist: Positioning names the target, benefit and differentiator
Staged launch with metrics per stage

checkpoint.title: Growth or burn?
checkpoint.scenario: A grocery-delivery startup grew orders 5x in six months with heavy discounts. Investors ask whether the business is healthy. Contribution per order is negative, and retention without discounts is unclear.
checkpoint.debrief: You looked past headline growth to unit economics, retention-based fit, sustainable loops and the right monetisation — the full business picture a PM must understand.

steps.prompt: Contribution per order is −₹40. What does that mean for scaling?

options.text: Each additional order loses money; scaling without fixing margins increases losses
options.why: Negative unit economics worsen with scale.
Only if costs fall with scale — prove that first.

options.text: It doesn't matter if orders grow

steps.prompt: How do you test whether there's real PMF beneath the discounts?

options.text: Compare retention of cohorts with reduced discounts and survey the most retained segment
options.why: Removes the subsidy to reveal true demand.

options.text: Increase discounts to see if orders grow

steps.prompt: Which growth approach is more sustainable than discounts?

options.text: A neighbourhood loop: shared group orders and referrals in housing societies that also batch deliveries
options.why: A loop that adds users and lowers delivery cost together.

steps.prompt: Which monetisation change best aligns price with value?

options.text: A delivery membership for frequent users plus a small-cart fee, so heavy users get value and small orders cover costs
options.why: Aligns pricing with usage and cost.

steps.explanation: Charge in line with value and cost.
